The mountain yellow-legged frog (Rana muscosa) is a high-elevation amphibian endemic to the Sierra Nevada and southern California mountain ranges, where it inhabits permanent streams and lakes. Embryonic development in this species is heavily influenced by cold thermal regimes typical of alpine environments. At a constant water temperature of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], eggs hatch after approximately 20 days [ab = approximately 20 days], a duration that reflects the metabolic constraints imposed by low temperatures on cleavage and organogenesis. The resulting hatchlings emerge at a remarkably small size, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], a figure derived from comparative data on related bufonids and consistent with the energetic limitations of yolk-dependent development in cold water. Following eclosion, the yolk-sac tadpoles remain non-feeding for a brief period, relying entirely on endogenous yolk reserves before transitioning to the exotrophic aquatic larval stage.

Once the gill-breathing tadpoles commence active feeding, they enter a prolonged phase of growth and development under the cool conditions of their montane habitat. Larval development culminates in metamorphosis, and field studies indicate that the time since birth at metamorphosis is approximately 912 days  when tadpoles are reared at 7 °C [T = 7 °C]. This extended larval period, spanning over two years, is unusually long compared to most North American ranids and likely represents an adaptation to the short growing seasons and low productivity of high-elevation water bodies. After completing the morphological transformation that includes tail resorption and limb bud development, the terrestrial juveniles emerge as froglets, though they remain small and vulnerable. The cost of this protracted development is offset by the advantage of emerging at a larger body size, which may improve overwinter survival in the harsh alpine environment.

Sexual maturation in Rana muscosa occurs gradually, with both sexes reaching a similar size threshold at the onset of puberty. The snout-vent length at puberty for females is 4 centimeters [Lp = 4 centimeters], a value that is identical to the snout-vent length at puberty for males, which is also 4 centimeters [Lp = 4 centimeters]. This congruence in size at gonadal maturation is somewhat unusual among anurans, where female-biased sexual size dimorphism often emerges before reproductive maturity. Body mass at puberty for females is approximately 7 grams [Wwp = approximately 7 grams], representing a substantial increase from the initial birth mass. The time since birth at puberty is estimated at 1460 days [tp = 1460 days] under the thermal conditions of 7 °C [T = 7 °C], indicating that individuals require roughly four years of growth and development before becoming reproductively viable. This delayed maturation is consistent with a slow life-history strategy typical of high-elevation ectotherms.

Adult body size in this species exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females attaining substantially larger dimensions than males. The ultimate snout-vent length for females reaches 6.8 centimeters [Li = 6.8 centimeters], whereas the ultimate snout-vent length for males is smaller at 5.9 centimeters [Li = 5.9 centimeters]. This difference in linear size translates into an even more dramatic disparity in body mass: the ultimate wet weight for females is 76 grams [Wwi = 76 grams], nearly double the ultimate wet weight for males, which is 40 grams [Wwi = 40 grams]. Such pronounced female-biased sexual size dimorphism is common in ranids and is thought to reflect fecundity selection, where larger females can produce larger or more numerous clutches. Longevity records indicate that the maximum lifespan in the wild is approximately 5110 days [am = approximately 5110 days] when maintained at an average environmental temperature of 10 °C [T = 10 °C], a notably long lifespan for a temperate anuran and one that underscores the species' slow pace of life.

Reproductive output in mountain yellow-legged frogs is modest but consistent with their cold-adapted, slow life history. In populations breeding at 15 °C [T = 15 °C], females produce approximately 2 to 3 clutches each year [F_R_i = approximately 2 to 3 clutches each year], with each clutch containing approximately 233 eggs [N_R_i = each clutch containing approximately 233 eggs]. This annual reproductive strategy, yielding a single large clutch rather than multiple smaller ones, is typical of high-elevation amphibians that face a narrow window of suitable breeding conditions. The eggs are deposited in gelatinous masses attached to submerged rocks in shallow, well-oxygenated water, where they undergo the 20-day incubation period previously described. The constraints of the alpine environment—short summers, low temperatures, and unpredictable weather—likely limit the opportunity for multiple breeding events per season, favoring instead the production of a single, relatively large clutch that maximizes per-event fecundity. This reproductive allocation pattern contrasts sharply with lowland congeners that often produce multiple clutches annually.
